C005.subject: Aspirin use
C005.object: cardiovascular event risk only in healthy adults with a 10-year ASCVD risk score ≥ 15% and without concurrent NSAID use
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Aspirin use cardiovascular event risk only in healthy adults with a 10-year ASCVD risk score ≥ 15% and without concurrent NSAID use]

[PATH:empirical] Post-hoc subgroup analysis of the ASPREE (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly) trial, stratified by baseline 10-year ASCVD risk score (≥15% vs. <15%) and NSAID use status — ASPREE is a large, placebo-controlled primary prevention trial in healthy older adults. Re-analyzing its data by the specified risk threshold and NSAID exclusion could directly test whether net cardiovascular benefit emerges only above that threshold, with bleeding risk offsetting benefit below it.

[PATH:empirical] Patient-level meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of aspirin for primary prevention (e.g., from the Antithrombotic Trialists' Collaboration) with individual 10-year ASCVD risk estimation and NSAID use data — Pooling individual participant data from multiple trials allows sufficiently powered subgroup analysis at the 15% risk threshold and assessment of effect modification by concurrent NSAID use, which is critical to confirm the hypothesized risk-stratified benefit.

[PATH:theoretical] Decision-analytic modeling study comparing aspirin's net benefit (cardiovascular events prevented vs. major bleeding events caused) across a continuous range of 10-year ASCVD risk scores, with and without NSAID interaction — A formal microsimulation or Markov model can quantify the threshold at which the benefit-risk trade-off becomes favorable, incorporating published risk equations and bleeding hazards, thereby providing theoretical support for the 15% cutoff and the NSAID interaction.

qualifier.tension: The benefit-risk trade-off may shift decisively in favor of net benefit only above this specific risk threshold, while bleeding risk offsets any benefit below it.

C006.subject: Aspirin use
C006.object: bleeding risk in healthy adults with elevated baseline risk
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Aspirin use bleeding risk in healthy adults with elevated baseline risk]

[PATH:empirical] ASPREE trial subgroup analyses (Aspirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly) focusing on participants with elevated baseline bleeding risk (e.g., history of GI ulcers, hypertension, or concurrent anticoagulant use) — This large, post-2000 RCT in Western populations provides direct randomized evidence on bleeding risk stratified by baseline risk factors, allowing confirmation or refutation of increased harm in high-risk subgroups.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of placebo-controlled aspirin primary prevention trials (e.g., ARRIVE, ASCEND, JPPP) with subgroup data on bleeding events in individuals with elevated cardiovascular or bleeding risk — Synthesizing existing trial data can increase statistical power to detect differential bleeding risk in high-risk subgroups, clarifying whether the effect is consistent across studies and populations.

[PATH:empirical] Pharmacoepidemiological cohort study using electronic health records from Western healthcare systems (e.g., UK Biobank or CPRD) comparing bleeding incidence in aspirin users vs. non-users among healthy adults with elevated baseline risk (e.g., HAS-BLED score ≥2) — Real-world observational data can complement trial evidence by capturing longer-term outcomes and broader populations, helping to confirm the hypothesized risk increase in routine clinical settings.

C007.subject: Aspirin use in healthy adults aged 70 or older
C007.object: intracranial hemorrhage risk more than gastrointestinal bleeding risk
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Aspirin use in healthy adults aged 70 or older intracranial hemorrhage risk more than gastrointestinal bleeding risk]

[PATH:empirical] ASPREE (ASPirin in Reducing Events in the Elderly) trial subgroup analysis on hemorrhagic outcomes by site (intracranial vs. gastrointestinal) — ASPREE is the largest randomized trial of aspirin in healthy adults ≥70, providing direct comparative risk data for intracranial and GI bleeding in this specific population.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of aspirin for primary prevention in adults ≥70, stratifying by bleeding type (intracranial hemorrhage vs. gastrointestinal bleeding) — Pooling results from multiple trials (e.g., ASPREE, JPPP, AAA) increases statistical power to detect differential risk increases and assess consistency across studies.

[PATH:empirical] Observational cohort study using Medicare claims data (2010–2020) to estimate incidence rates of intracranial hemorrhage and gastrointestinal bleeding among aspirin users vs. non-users aged ≥70 — Large-scale real-world data can validate trial findings and provide age-specific absolute risk differences, accounting for baseline comorbidity and concurrent medication use.

scope.domain: primary prevention in older healthy adults

C008.subject: Aspirin use
C008.object: major bleeding risk in healthy adults

[PATH:empirical] A large-scale, long-term randomized controlled trial (e.g., ASPREE or similar) stratified by baseline bleeding risk in healthy adults aged 50-70, with extended follow-up for major bleeding events — Directly tests the hypothesis by comparing aspirin vs. placebo in a healthy primary prevention population, providing definitive evidence on bleeding risk across different risk levels.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of individual participant data from primary prevention trials (2000-2020) focusing on major bleeding events in low-risk subgroups (e.g., without hypertension, diabetes, or prior GI issues) — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the null effect holds in truly healthy adults, addressing the disputed status and scope of the hypothesis.

C011.subject: Aspirin use
C011.object: only in healthy adults with 5-year cardiovascular risk ≥10% when dose is ≤100 mg and follow-up exceeds 5 years
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Aspirin use only in healthy adults with 5-year cardiovascular risk ≥10% when dose is ≤100 mg and follow-up exceeds 5 years]

[PATH:empirical] ASPREE trial subgroup analysis by baseline cardiovascular risk and aspirin dose — The ASPREE trial provides long-term follow-up data in healthy older adults; re-analyzing subgroups with 5-year CV risk ≥10% and doses ≤100 mg could directly test the net benefit threshold and duration effect.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials on low-dose aspirin in primary prevention stratified by 5-year CV risk and follow-up duration — A comprehensive meta-analysis that pools trials like AAA, JPAD, and ASCEND, specifically stratified by baseline risk ≥10% and follow-up >5 years, can assess whether net benefit emerges only under these conditions.

[PATH:empirical] Causal inference modeling using observational data (e.g., UK Biobank) with dose, duration, and risk-stratified propensity scores — Observational data with large sample sizes and long follow-up allow estimation of aspirin's net benefit in the specific high-risk subgroup, controlling for confounders, to confirm or refute the hypothesis under real-world conditions.

scope.domain: primary prevention with dose and duration stratification

qualifier.geographic: high-income countries with similar cardiovascular risk profiles

C012.subject: Aspirin use
C012.object: in healthy adults for primary prevention irrespective of dose and follow-up duration
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Aspirin use in healthy adults for primary prevention irrespective of dose and follow-up duration]

[PATH:literature] A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing low-dose aspirin (≤100 mg daily) versus placebo or no aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events and major bleeding in healthy adults, stratified by follow-up duration (e.g., <5 years vs. ≥5 years). — Directly tests the hypothesis by aggregating high-quality trial data across different doses and follow-up periods, enabling assessment of net benefit (e.g., reduction in myocardial infarction/stroke vs. increase in major bleeding).

[PATH:empirical] A large-scale prospective cohort study (e.g., using UK Biobank or NHANES) with propensity-score matching to compare long-term outcomes (cardiovascular events, gastrointestinal bleeding, hemorrhagic stroke, all-cause mortality) between healthy adults who self-select to take aspirin regularly versus those who do not, with sensitivity analyses by dose and duration. — Provides real-world evidence on net benefit in a general healthy population, addressing limitations of trial generalizability and capturing long-term effects beyond typical trial follow-up.

[PATH:theoretical] A decision-analytic model (e.g., Markov microsimulation) incorporating baseline cardiovascular risk, bleeding risk, aspirin dose-response curves, and time-varying hazard ratios from published trials, calibrated to global populations to estimate net benefit in quality-adjusted life years across different follow-up horizons. — Allows formal quantification of net benefit under explicit assumptions about dose and duration, clarifying whether any plausible scenario supports the hypothesis or whether it is uniformly refuted.
